title: Why Does Cilantro Taste Like Soap to 1 in 8 People?
description:
Why does cilantro taste like soap to some people and fresh to others? See how aldehydes, the OR6A2 smell gene, a surprisingly tiny genetic effect and what you grew up eating all shape the soapy cilantro taste, plus the crushing trick that can soften it.

Sources:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.2096
https://www.nbcnews.com/health/body-odd/who-hates-cilantro-study-aims-find-out-flna775011

topic: Why does cilantro taste like soap to some people?
script: Your cilantro tastes like soap, to one in eight people, and you might be one. Same leaf, same taco. You get something fresh and lemony. Your friend gets a mouthful of dish soap. So who's right? Weirdly, you both are. And the answer starts in your nose. People have used this herb for thousands of years, all the way back to the Babylonians. And the haters have been loud. Before soap was the go-to insult, people said it smelled like bedbugs. Chef Julia Child once said, she'd pick it out of her food, and throw it on the floor. So how many people really dislike it? One Canadian study asked nearly fourteen hundred young adults. Dislike ran from just three percent, all the way up to twenty-one percent, depending on family background. And some of the lowest numbers came from people with Hispanic and South Asian roots, whose cooking uses cilantro all the time. Now, let's zoom in on one leaf. That smell is a big mix of chemicals, and some of the main ones are called aldehydes. Picture a long chain of carbon atoms, with one little oxygen on the end. One of them, called decenal, gets described as soapy, fatty and pungent. Here's the twist. Soap makers use aldehydes too. Cilantro and soap really do share a family of smells. Scientists still aren't sure which exact molecule is to blame. So why does only your friend notice? Scientists suspect this is mostly about smell, not taste. When you chew, scents float up the back of your throat, and into your nose. Up there, you've got hundreds of kinds of smell sensors. Think of them as tiny locks, and every scent molecule as a key. In twenty twelve, researchers at twenty-three and me, looked at the DNA of about twenty-five thousand people. They asked one question. Does cilantro taste like soap to you? And they found one tiny spot in the DNA, right next to a cluster of smell genes. One of those genes is called O R six A two, and it builds a lock that's great at catching aldehydes. Some people's noses may pick up that soapy note, a lot more loudly. Case closed, right? Not quite. Here's the number nobody expects. That spot explains only about half a percent of who tastes soap and who doesn't. Half of one percent! Another twin study turned up more genes, including some linked to bitter taste. So there's no single soap gene. It's a small nudge, mixed with everything else about you. Like what you ate growing up. Remember those low numbers? If cilantro was in your food from day one, you've had a lot of practice. The lead researcher said this isn't like your height. You aren't stuck with it. Scientists say eating it again and again, can slowly soften the soap. And there's a kitchen trick. Crush the leaves. Crushing releases enzymes, that break those soapy aldehydes into milder smells. That's why food scientists suggest starting with cilantro pesto. So next time your friend picks it out of the salsa, go easy on them. They aren't being picky. Their nose is finding something real, that yours might be missing. Next up, how do dolphins sleep without drowning?
key_facts: 23andMe GWAS (Eriksson et al. 2012, arXiv 1209.2096): 14,604 discovery + 11,851 replication participants; 12.4% of all respondents in Table 3 reported soapy taste (2299/18495), about 1 in 8
SNP rs72921001 lies near a cluster of eight olfactory receptor genes including OR6A2, which has high binding specificity for aldehydes; (E)-2-decenal described as soapy, fatty, pungent (same paper)
The SNP explains only about 0.5% of the variance in perceiving soapy taste; the paper says dislike is suspected, not proven, to be odor driven
Mauer & El-Sohemy 2012 (Flavour), via NBC: nearly 1,400 Canadian young adults; dislike 3% (Middle Eastern) to 21% (East Asian), Hispanic 4%, South Asian 7%; early exposure likely helps

Twin study (Knaapila et al., 527 twins) found more genes including two tied to bitter taste; lead author Eriksson: 'It isn't like your height'; McGee: crushing releases enzymes that convert the aldehydes to milder aromas; cilantro pesto suggestion (WGBH/NPR)

Julia Child on Larry King (2002, via Tasting Table): she'd pick it out and throw it on the floor. Described as smelling of bedbugs before 'soapy' (Charles Spence, Live Science). Babylonian use (Gastropod)
